title: Crossing the Rubicon: How Caesar Ended the Roman Republic
alt_titles: Julius Caesar: From the Rubicon to the Ides of March
The Five Years That Ended the Roman Republic
description_summary: In January 49 BC, Julius Caesar led his army across the Rubicon and into civil war. Five years later he was dead. This is the story of how one river crossing brought down the Roman Republic, told from the ancient sources.

scenes.narration: In January 49 BC, on the edge of northern Italy, Gaius Julius Caesar stopped beside a small river called the Rubicon. Behind him were soldiers who had followed him through years of war in Gaul. Ahead lay Italy itself, where Roman law forbade a governor to lead his army.

shots.file: File:Gustave Boulanger, Jules-César arrivé au Rubicon, 1854, Musée Picardie.jpg
shots.query: Caesar arrives at the Rubicon Boulanger
shots.caption: Caesar arrives at the Rubicon, Gustave Boulanger, 1854

shots.file: File:Wilhelm Trübner - Caesar am Rubicon - 8522 - Österreichische Galerie Belvedere.jpg
shots.caption: Caesar at the Rubicon, Wilhelm Trübner, 19th century

scenes.narration: Crossing that river with his troops would be an act of war against the Roman state. Ancient writers say he hesitated, then gave the order to cross. Five years later he was dead, killed by men he knew well, and the Roman Republic was nearing its end.

shots.file: File:The "Tusculum portrait", a rare bust of Julius Caesar in his lifetime, 45 - 43 BC, Moi, Auguste, Empereur de Rome exhibition, Grand Palais, Paris - 14628246546.jpg
shots.caption: The Tusculum portrait of Julius Caesar, made around 45 to 43 BC

shots.file: File:Jean Fouquet - Caesar Crossing the Rubicon - WGA08034.jpg
shots.caption: Caesar crossing the Rubicon, Jean Fouquet, 15th century

scenes.narration: This is the story of those five years: how one river crossing started a civil war, how Caesar won it, and how it ended in a hall full of senators on the Ides of March.

shots.file: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - The Death of Caesar - Walters 37884.jpg
shots.caption: The Death of Caesar, Jean-Léon Gérôme, 1859 to 1867
A coin issued by Brutus celebrating the Ides of March

scenes.narration: For centuries, Rome had been a republic. Power was shared between elected officials and the Senate, and no one person was meant to rule. Romans had expelled their last king in 509 BC, and the very idea of a king was hated.

shots.query: Cicero denounces Catiline Maccari fresco Senate
shots.caption: The Roman Senate, imagined by Cesare Maccari, 1880s
The Roman Forum, heart of the Republic

scenes.narration: By Caesar's lifetime, that system was under strain. Rome's empire had grown enormously, and its armies were commanded by ambitious generals. Their soldiers were often more loyal to their commander than to the Senate. Caesar would become the most successful of them all.

shots.caption: A bust of Julius Caesar, Uffizi Gallery

shots.file: File:Map of the Ancient Rome at Caesar time (with conquests)-en.svg
shots.caption: Rome's territory in Caesar's time, with his conquests

scenes.narration: In the 50s BC, he led Roman armies in Gaul, a region covering much of modern France and Belgium. The campaigns lasted most of a decade, and they made him rich, famous and very powerful. In 52 BC, he crushed a great uprising led by the Gallic chieftain Vercingetorix.

shots.caption: Vercingetorix surrenders to Caesar, Lionel Royer, 1899
Map of Caesar's campaigns in Gaul

scenes.narration: Caesar had not risen alone. He had worked with two powerful allies: Pompey the Great, Rome's most celebrated general, and Marcus Crassus, one of its richest men. Historians call their informal alliance the First Triumvirate.

shots.file: File:Pompey the Great, mid 1st cent. BCE, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Copenhagen (36023583270).jpg
shots.caption: Pompey the Great, bust in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek

shots.file: File:First Triumvirate of Caesar, Crassius and Pompey.jpg
shots.caption: Caesar, Crassus and Pompey, the so-called First Triumvirate

scenes.narration: But the partnership began to fall apart. Caesar's daughter Julia, who had married Pompey, died. Then in 53 BC Crassus was killed fighting the Parthians at Carrhae. The two personal ties that had held Caesar and Pompey together were gone.

shots.caption: Bust traditionally identified as Marcus Crassus
The Parthians, who defeated Crassus at Carrhae

scenes.narration: Pompey drew closer to Caesar's enemies in the Senate. They demanded that Caesar give up his army and his command. Many historians think that, without an army to protect him, he would have faced prosecution by his enemies in Rome. For Caesar, giving in could mean ruin.

shots.caption: Another view of the Copenhagen bust of Pompey
The Senate house in Rome

scenes.narration: In early January 49 BC, the Senate passed an emergency decree against him. It effectively made him an enemy of the state. Caesar was in the north with his troops. He could obey and give up everything he had won, or he could fight. He had a decision to make.

shots.caption: The Roman world in 49 BC
Caesar, painted by Eugène Yvon, 1875

scenes.narration: The Rubicon was a small river near the Adriatic coast. It marked the boundary between the province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy. A governor could command troops in his province. Leading them across that line into Italy was treason. A governor who did so could be declared a public enemy.

shots.caption: Ancient Italy and its Roman roads
The river now identified as the Rubicon

scenes.narration: The ancient writers Suetonius and Appian both describe Caesar pausing at the river. Both report that he used a phrase that became famous: the die is cast. Whether he said exactly those words, we cannot know. But the meaning was clear. There was no going back.

shots.caption: Caesar crosses the Rubicon, a later illustration
Caesar crossing the Rubicon, 19th-century illustration

scenes.narration: He crossed. Within days his troops had seized Ariminum, modern Rimini, and other towns. News reached Rome, and the city prepared for war. His opponents had expected him to back down. Instead, he was marching south.

shots.caption: Caesar crossing the Rubicon, a later print
Ariminum, modern Rimini, one of the first towns Caesar took

scenes.narration: Pompey and many senators decided they could not hold Italy. They withdrew across the sea to Greece to gather their forces there. Caesar now controlled Rome and the Italian peninsula, and the whole Roman world had to choose a side.

shots.file: File:Pompey the Great, c. A.D. 30—50, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Copenhagen (13647207644).jpg
shots.caption: Pompey the Great, a portrait made after his death

shots.query: Brundisium ancient port Brindisi Roman column
shots.caption: Brundisium, the port on the route to Greece

scenes.narration: The war spread across the Roman world. In 48 BC, the two sides met at Pharsalus in Greece. Caesar's army was outnumbered, but his veterans were hardened by years of fighting in Gaul. Pompey was decisively defeated. It was the turning point of the war, and Pompey's cause never recovered.

shots.caption: The Battle of Pharsalus, as imagined by a later artist
The Battle of Pharsalus, 48 BC

scenes.narration: Pompey fled to Egypt, hoping to find shelter. Instead, he was killed there. The greatest general of his generation, once Caesar's ally and son-in-law, died far from Rome. With Pompey gone, the war against Caesar lost its most famous leader, but not its supporters.

shots.caption: The Spada statue, long thought to show Pompey
Alexandria, capital of Egypt at the time

scenes.narration: Fighting went on for several more years against Pompey's surviving supporters. By 45 BC, Caesar had beaten them all. He returned to Rome with no rival left standing, and with power no Roman had held for centuries.

shots.caption: Julius Caesar, painted by Peter Paul Rubens
The Triumphs of Caesar, Andrea Mantegna, 15th century

scenes.narration: Caesar was made dictator, an emergency office that normally lasted a short time. He held it again and again. Shortly before his death, he was named dictator for life, dictator perpetuo. To many senators, that title sounded alarmingly permanent.

shots.caption: A silver denarius of Julius Caesar
A portrait of Julius Caesar

scenes.narration: His portrait appeared on coins. He took decisions without consulting the Senate and controlled the treasury. There were rumours that he wanted to be king. To his enemies, he already looked like a king in everything but name.

shots.query: Julius Caesar lifetime denarius portrait 44 BC
shots.caption: A coin with Caesar's portrait, 44 BC

shots.query: Julius Caesar statue Rome Via dei Fori Imperiali
shots.caption: Statue of Caesar in Rome

scenes.narration: Some Romans welcomed peace and order after years of bloodshed and civil war. Others, especially in the Senate, felt their power and their Republic slipping away. Among them were men Caesar knew well, and who had seen him at close quarters.

shots.caption: A Roman senator in a toga

shots.query: Marcus Junius Brutus bust Palazzo Massimo
shots.caption: A bust thought to show Marcus Junius Brutus

scenes.narration: A plot took shape in secret over the following weeks. At least sixty men were involved, and some accounts suggest more. The leaders were Gaius Cassius Longinus and Marcus Junius Brutus, a man Caesar knew well. Others included Gaius Trebonius and Decimus Brutus.

shots.caption: Brutus, from a coin issued by his forces
A coin of Gaius Cassius Longinus

scenes.narration: Ancient writers tell of warnings. A soothsayer named Spurinna is said to have told Caesar that danger would come no later than the Ides of March. His wife Calpurnia is said to have dreamed of him covered in blood, and begged him to stay at home.

shots.caption: Calpurnia, Caesar's wife, as imagined by a later artist

shots.query: Julius Caesar soothsayer Ides of March illustration
shots.caption: A soothsayer warns Caesar, later illustration

scenes.narration: On the morning itself, someone is said to have pressed a note into Caesar's hand warning him of the plot. In the crush of people around him, he did not read it. He went on towards the Senate meeting.

shots.query: Julius Caesar on the way to the Senate Ides of March painting
shots.caption: Caesar on his way to the Senate, as imagined by a later artist
Remains of the Theatre of Pompey complex in Rome

scenes.narration: On the fifteenth of March, 44 BC, Caesar went to a meeting of the Senate. It was held in a hall that was part of the Theatre of Pompey. There, the conspirators surrounded him and attacked with daggers. Ancient writers counted twenty-three wounds.

shots.file: File:Vincenzo Camuccini - La morte di Cesare.jpg
shots.caption: The Death of Caesar, Vincenzo Camuccini, 1798

shots.file: File:Karl Theodor von Piloty Murder of Caesar 1865.jpg
shots.caption: The Murder of Caesar, Karl von Piloty, 1865

scenes.narration: According to Suetonius, a doctor who examined the body concluded that only one of the wounds had been fatal. The attack was fast, confused and brutal, and it was over in minutes.

shots.query: Death of Julius Caesar painting Senate conspirators
shots.caption: The conspirators around Caesar, as imagined by a later artist
A reconstruction of the Theatre of Pompey complex

scenes.narration: His last words are disputed. Suetonius wrote that Caesar died without a word. Plutarch recorded a different moment. What is certain is that the most powerful man in Rome lay dead. He had died in a hall that bore the name of his old rival.

shots.caption: Another version of Gérôme's Death of Caesar

shots.query: Largo di Torre Argentina Curia of Pompey
shots.caption: The site of the Curia of Pompey in Rome today

scenes.narration: The conspirators believed they had saved the Republic from a tyrant. Brutus even issued coins showing two daggers and the words EID MAR, the Ides of March. But the killing did not bring back the old Republic. It led to more civil war.

shots.caption: A gold EID MAR coin in the British Museum
The reverse of an Ides of March coin

scenes.narration: At Caesar's funeral, Mark Antony stirred up the crowds, and public anger turned against the assassins. Caesar's great-nephew and adopted heir, the nineteen-year-old Octavian, began to gather support. In 42 BC, Brutus and Cassius were defeated at Philippi and died there.

shots.query: Mark Antony oration Caesar funeral painting
shots.caption: Mark Antony at Caesar's funeral, later painting
The young Octavian, Caesar's heir

scenes.narration: Within two years of his murder, Caesar was officially declared a god by the Roman state. The man killed for acting like a king was now worshipped in temples. For the conspirators, it was the opposite of everything they had hoped for.

shots.query: Temple of Divus Julius Roman Forum
shots.caption: The Temple of the Divine Julius in the Roman Forum
A coin honouring the deified Caesar

scenes.narration: Over the years that followed, Octavian outlasted every rival. He took the name Augustus and became Rome's first emperor. The men who killed Caesar to stop one man ruling Rome had cleared the way for exactly that.

shots.caption: Augustus of Prima Porta, statue of Rome's first emperor
Augustus, the name Octavian took as emperor

scenes.narration: Today, crossing the Rubicon still means taking a step that cannot be undone. Caesar's own step helped to end a Republic that had lasted nearly five centuries. Sources and image credits are in the description.

shots.caption: The Roman world at Caesar's death, 44 BC
Statue of Julius Caesar in Rimini
